newsitem.title: USA: Rubin warns Japan over trade ahead of Asia trip.
newsitem.headline: Rubin warns Japan over trade ahead of Asia trip.

text.p: By Rich Miller, U.S. Economics Correspondent
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin warned Japan on Wednesday that a renewed rise in its trade surplus could cause friction with the United States and the rest of the world.
"If you had a resurgence of a trade surplus ... it has the potential of doing that," he told the New York Stock Exchange Board of Directors here.

Speaking on the eve of a six-day trip to Asia that will take him to Japan, the Philippines and Vietnam, Rubin urged Tokyo to promote domestic demand for its products and strengthen its battered banking industry, saying that was critical to the region's financial success.
"Our goal is clear -- to foster growth in Asia, which will, in turn, promote global growth," he said. "The end result will be increased U.S. exports, more high- paying jobs and greater prosperity."
Rubin said he was encouraged by the progress that Japan has made in reducing its trade surplus in recent years but he made clear that the United States did not want that reversed.

Japan's trade surplus rose in February for the first time in two years, expanding by 6.5 percent from a year earlier, as the weakness of the Japanese yen against the dollar helped make the nation's exports more competitive on world markets.
Rubin told reporters after his speech that the strong dollar had benefitted the United States by keeping inflation low. But he added that the U.S. currency has been strong for "quite some time."
Some analysts have read Rubin's remarks about the dollar, and his apparent stepped-up criticism of Japan, as a sign that the Treasury wants the U.S. currency to drop against the yen.
"Our Treasury, at least implicitly, is now calling for (a stronger yen)," said Fred Bergsten, a former U.S. official who now heads the Institute of International Economics think tank.

But Rubin vehemently denied that his remarks were meant to trigger any movement in the dollar or other currencies. "My comments absolutely, absolutely, are not intended directly or indirectly to call for any movement of any currency," he said.

Rubin, who will meet Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in Tokyo on Friday, will turn his attention to the regional economy on Saturday and Sunday when he attends a meeting of Asia-Pacific finance ministers in the Philippines.

He said he expects to reach an agreement there on a set of principles to guide development of capital markets and enhance the role of the private sector in financing the construction of roads, bridges and other infrastructure in Asia.
Rubin said he will also seek the group's support for a successful end of World Trade Organization negotiations to open up the financial services industry to more competition.
Washington wants to strike a deal by the end of this year. But for that to occur, key emerging markets must significantly improve on their offers of increased access, he said.
Following the meeting of the 18-member Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation group, Rubin will travel to Vietnam for a two-day visit there.
He will be the highest-ranking U.S. economic policymaker to visit Vietnam in decades in the latest step toward normalizing ties with America's former wartime foe.

While in Hanoi, Rubin will sign an agreement to reschedule some $145 million of debts run up by the former government of South Vietnam and will discuss what other steps the two countries can take to normalize relations.
"The United States, in both the government and the private sector, has much to offer to promote growth in Vietnam," he said.
But, he added that Vietnam must press ahead with reforms and be willing to open up its markets substantially in return.
